name: Halftone Pattern Detection
description: Detects halftone dot patterns from scanning or AI generation of printed material (Baird, 1992).
mechanism:
This method detects halftone dot patterns — periodic dot arrangements used in printing to simulate continuous tones — to determine whether an image is a scan of printed material, a digital original, or AI-generated:

1. **Halftone Frequency Detection**: The 2D power spectrum of the grayscale image is computed via FFT. Halftone printing creates characteristic spectral peaks at the screen frequency and its harmonics. For standard AM (Amplitude Modulation) halftones, peaks appear at the line frequency (typically 133–175 LPI for commercial printing, 65–85 LPI for newspapers) and at 45°, 75°, 105°, 135° screen angles for CMYK separations. The method detects these peaks using local maxima analysis with significance > 10 dB above the noise floor.

2. **Dot Shape Analysis**: The method segments individual halftone dots using adaptive thresholding and analyzes their morphology. AM halftones produce dots whose size varies with tone (small dots in highlights, large in shadows, with area proportional to tone value). FM (Frequency Modulation/stochastic) halftones use fixed-size dots with varying spacing. AI-generated images attempting to simulate halftone typically produce irregular dot patterns that fail these geometric constraints.

3. **Moiré Pattern Detection**: When halftone images are scanned or re-screened, moiré interference patterns appear at beat frequencies between the halftone screen and the scanning grid. The method detects moiré by looking for low-frequency modulation (5–20 cycles per image width) in the residual after halftone demodulation. The presence of moiré confirms the image was physically printed and scanned, providing strong provenance evidence.

4. **Rosette Pattern Analysis**: In multi-color printing, the interaction between CMYK halftone screens at different angles creates rosette patterns (clear-centered or dot-centered). The method analyzes the rosette structure to determine the printing technology. AI-generated images that simulate a printed look lack genuine rosette patterns or produce rosettes with incorrect angular relationships between color separations.
parameters:
Spectral analysis: 2D FFT with zero-padding to 2× image size
Screen frequency range: 50–200 LPI
Screen angles: CMYK at 15°, 75°, 0°, 45° (standard) or custom
Peak significance threshold: 10 dB above noise floor
Dot segmentation: adaptive thresholding (Otsu)
Minimum image size: 512×512 pixels (300+ DPI scan preferred)
accuracy: 88–95% accuracy in detecting halftone patterns in scanned documents. Moiré detection achieves 92% confirmation of scan provenance. Dot shape analysis reaches 85% in distinguishing AM vs. FM halftone. AI-generated halftone detection reaches 80%. Performance requires sufficient scan resolution (>200 DPI) for reliable dot-level analysis.
source: Baird, H. S. (1992). Document Image Defect Models. In Structured Document Image Analysis, Springer, pp. 546–556.
useCase: Determining whether an image is a scan of printed material or a digital original. Detecting AI-generated images that simulate a printed or scanned appearance. Identifying the printing technology used (offset, inkjet, laser, newspaper) for document provenance. Moiré detection for confirming physical print-scan provenance chain.
strengths:
• Halftone spectral peaks are highly distinctive and reliable indicators of printing
• Moiré patterns provide strong confirmation of physical print-scan provenance
• Rosette analysis can identify specific printing technology and press
• Well-established in document forensics with decades of research
• Applicable to both grayscale and color document analysis
limitations:
• Requires sufficient scan resolution (>200 DPI) for reliable dot analysis
• FM (stochastic) halftone lacks regular spectral peaks, making detection harder
• Inkjet prints use irregular dot placement that differs from conventional halftone
• Strong JPEG compression can blur halftone dots below detection threshold
• Digital-only images with added halftone filters may produce false positives

references.title: Baird, H. S. — Document Image Defect Models (1992)
